Creating The Right Mood For a Performance; Series 1 Learning to Move Beyond Your Personal Feelings… A great performance is not only about singing the right notes, playing the right chords, or remembering the arrangement. It is also about creating and communicating the right emotional atmosphere. As singers, choristers and musicians, we sometimes arrive at a performance carrying emotions that have nothing to do with what we are about to perform. You may be tired, discouraged, worried about something happening at home, disappointed by something that happened during rehearsal, or simply not feeling energetic. Yet the audience is waiting. The music still needs to communicate. This is where professional emotional discipline becomes important. YOUR PERSONAL MOOD IS NOT ALWAYS THE MOOD OF THE PERFORMANCE. One of the most important lessons I have learned as a music director, music instructor, mentor, producer and voice coach is that how you feel personally and what the performance requires are not always the same thing. Imagine a singer who has had a difficult morning but is expected to lead a joyful worship song. Or a choir that has just experienced tension during rehearsal but needs to walk on stage and communicate unity and warmth. Or a saxophonist who is mentally distracted but has been assigned a powerful solo that requires confidence and energy. The challenge is not necessarily to pretend that your personal feelings don’t exist. The challenge is to recognize your emotional state, manage it, and deliberately enter the emotional world required by the music. Music Carries Emotion Music is more than sound. A melody can communicate joy. A minor progression can create sadness or tension. A rhythmic groove can create excitement. A slow musical passage can create reflection. A powerful crescendo can communicate anticipation, triumph or intensity. Therefore, performers must ask: “What should the audience feel when they hear this?” That question can change the way you perform. A singer shouldn’t simply sing the lyrics. They should understand the emotion behind them. A pianist shouldn’t simply play the notes. They should understand the character of the music. A drummer shouldn’t simply keep time. They should understand how rhythm contributes to the atmosphere. A choir shouldn’t simply sing together. They should communicate a collective emotional message. SOMETIMES YOU HAVE TO COME OUT OF YOUR MOOD… This does not mean suppressing your emotions or pretending to be someone you are not. It means developing the ability to transition emotionally. You might enter rehearsal feeling quiet and withdrawn, but the music requires energy. You might feel excited personally, but the piece requires calmness and sensitivity. You might be frustrated with something that happened before the performance, but the audience needs to experience peace, joy or confidence through your performance. Professional performers learn how to make this transition intentionally. Think of it as changing musical gears. You don’t remain in the same emotional gear throughout every performance. “A professional performer does not always perform from the mood they came with; they learn to enter the mood the music requires and invite the audience into it.”— Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #EmotionalWellBeing #ImprovedDisciplineAndPatience #musicians #musicperformance #performance #performancetips #rehearsal #rehearsals #selfCare #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers #stagepresence #Victoradenola
